quote: You can also call a tile another player discards if it completes a pung, kong, or quint you're building — or completes your whole hand — without waiting for your own turn.
issue: Two limits are missing, and these are the ones my students trip over most. You can't call a discard for a single or a pair unless it gives you Mahjong. And on a concealed hand you can't call anything except the tile that finishes the hand. Sextets are missing too.
suggested_fix: You can also call a tile another player discards if it completes a pung, kong, quint or sextet you're building, or if it completes your whole hand. You can't call a discard for a single or a pair unless it gives you Mahjong, and on a concealed hand you can only call the tile that finishes it.

quote: When you call a tile, you expose that group face-up in front of your rack so everyone can see it.
issue: Beginners almost always draw from the wall after calling. It's worth one more sentence.
suggested_fix: When you call a tile, you expose that group face-up in front of your rack, then discard. You don't draw from the wall on that turn.

quote: If a discarded tile completes a pung, kong, or quint you're building, you can call it out of turn instead of waiting to draw it.
issue: Same gaps as the Beginner Guide (sextets, no calling for singles or pairs, concealed hands). Also nothing about timing. You have to call before the next player takes their tile.
suggested_fix: If a discarded tile completes a pung, kong, quint or sextet you're building, you can call it out of turn. Call it before the next player draws. You can't call a discard for a single or a pair, or for a concealed hand, unless it gives you Mahjong.
certainty: Sure on the limits. Fairly sure on timing, since some groups say 'before the next player racks or discards'

quote: If two players want the same discard, Mahjong beats a pung, kong, or quint call. Otherwise the player who would play next gets it.
issue: 'Otherwise' sounds like it only applies to exposures. If two players both call Mahjong on the same tile, the one whose turn comes next also gets it.
suggested_fix: If two players want the same discard, a Mahjong call beats any other call. If both want it for the same reason (both for Mahjong, or both for an exposure), the player whose turn comes next gets it.

quote: A player with a dead hand keeps drawing and discarding, but can no longer win or call tiles for that round.
issue: Missing that a dead hand still pays if someone else wins. New players think they're off the hook.
suggested_fix: A player with a dead hand keeps drawing and discarding, but can no longer win or call tiles for that round. If someone else wins, the dead hand still pays.

quote: A hand can go dead — for example, if you call Mahjong on a hand that doesn't match the card, or your tile count is wrong.
issue: Mahjong in error is more complicated than this. Whether the hand is dead depends on whether you've exposed your tiles and whether others have already thrown in their hands. Saying it this flatly will scare beginners off calling at all.
suggested_fix: A hand can go dead, for example if your tile count is wrong, or if you call Mahjong by mistake and lay your hand down. If you catch the mistake before you expose your tiles, many groups let it go. Ask your group how they handle it.

quote: Ask your group who deals next — it can differ from table to table.
issue: Under standard rules the deal passes to the right after every hand, including a wall game. Keeping the same dealer is a house rule.
suggested_fix: Under standard rules the deal passes to the right after every hand, even when nobody wins. A few groups keep the same dealer after a wall game, so ask.

quote: everyone stacks their tiles into a double row in front of them
issue: Fine, but giving the size helps. If someone's wall comes out short, you know tiles are missing.
suggested_fix: everyone builds a wall two tiles high and 19 tiles long in front of them

quote: A standard set has only four of each tile, so a quint always includes at least one joker.
issue: Not true for Flowers. There are eight in a set, so a quint of Flowers can be all real tiles.
suggested_fix: A standard set has only four of each suit, Wind and Dragon tile, so a quint of those always includes at least one joker. Flowers are the exception, since there are eight of them.

quote: the word that ends the game
issue: It ends the hand, not the game. You keep playing hands all afternoon.
suggested_fix: the word that ends the hand

issue: Words a beginner will hear the first night that aren't here: Sextet, Soap (the White Dragon, also used as a zero in the year hands), Flower, East (the dealer), Dead hand, Courtesy pass, Blind pass, Singles and Pairs. Soap as zero confuses every class I teach.
suggested_fix: Add short entries for each.

quote: On the last pass, you may pass "blind": you can hand along tiles you just received without looking at them.
issue: This only covers the first Charleston. Blind passing is allowed on the first left (last pass of the first Charleston) and on the last right (last pass of the second). You can pass one, two or all three of the incoming tiles blind and make up the rest from your rack.
suggested_fix: On the last pass of each round (the first left, and the last right if you play a second round) you may pass 'blind': instead of choosing all three tiles from your rack, you can pass along one, two or all three of the tiles you're receiving without looking at them.
certainty: Sure on which passes. Fairly sure on the one-to-three part

quote: If anyone says no, you skip straight to play.
issue: Stopping the second Charleston doesn't cancel the courtesy pass. That still happens.
suggested_fix: If anyone says no, the second round is skipped. You can still do the courtesy pass.

quote: After the Charleston, players sitting across from each other may agree to a courtesy pass, swapping anywhere from zero to three tiles.
issue: Add what happens if the two players want different numbers (you go with the smaller one). And jokers can't go in the courtesy pass either.
suggested_fix: After the Charleston, players sitting across from each other may agree to a courtesy pass of zero to three tiles. If you want different numbers, you go with the smaller one. Jokers can't be passed here either.

quote: The card marks these hands (look for the C).
issue: Every hand on the card has either a C or an X. X means you may expose groups (you don't have to). Worth saying a C hand can still win on a discard for the very last tile and still counts as concealed. Also, the C isn't a bonus; the point value is printed next to the hand.
suggested_fix: Every hand on the card is marked C (concealed) or X (exposures allowed). On a C hand you can't expose anything, but you can still win by calling a discard for your final tile. The C or X tells you how to play the hand; the points are the number printed next to it.
certainty: Sure on C and X. Fairly sure on the last-tile part

quote: Many hands also pay double when played without any jokers.
issue: Any hand made without jokers is doubled (jokerless), except Singles and Pairs hands, which can't use jokers anyway. The card doesn't mark these separately. Also the doubles add up: a self-drawn jokerless hand is four times the value from everyone.
suggested_fix: If you win without using any jokers, the value of the hand is doubled. The exception is Singles and Pairs hands, since they can't use jokers anyway. These doubles add up, so a jokerless hand you draw yourself pays four times from each player.

quote: Your card and your group will tell you which of these apply.
issue: These payment rules are standard. What varies is the extras some groups add, like a dealer bonus. There's no dealer bonus under standard rules.
suggested_fix: These are the standard payments. Some groups add their own extras (for example, the dealer paying or collecting double), so ask before you play for money.

where: Jokers > What a joker can do
quote: it can stand in for almost any other tile in a pung, kong, or quint (a group of three, four, or five matching tiles)
issue: Sextets are missing.
suggested_fix: it can stand in for almost any other tile in a pung, kong, quint or sextet (a group of three, four, five or six matching tiles)

where: Jokers > What a joker can't do
quote: Some hands go further and don't allow jokers anywhere at all; the card marks which ones, so it's worth checking before you build around one.
issue: As far as I know the card doesn't use a special mark for this. It comes from how the hand is built, mostly the Singles and Pairs section, where every group is a single or a pair. I'd check this against this year's card before publishing.
suggested_fix: Some hands, like the ones in the Singles and Pairs section, are made only of singles and pairs, so jokers can't be used anywhere in them. Check the card before you build around a joker.

quote: you can swap on your turn
issue: Say when in the turn. Beginners try to do it after they've discarded.
suggested_fix: you can swap on your turn, after you draw and before you discard. You can swap more than one joker in the same turn.

quote: In most groups, you say the name of a tile out loud when you discard it, so everyone can hear it.
issue: This is a rule, not just a habit. Every group I've played with does it. Also worth saying that once a tile is named and on the table, it's discarded.
suggested_fix: Say the name of each tile out loud as you discard it, so everyone hears it. Once you've named it and set it down, you can't take it back. (Some beginner tables allow it, so ask.)

issue: Two things missing. No table talk: don't tell people what you're building or which tiles you need. And call promptly: if you want a discard, say so before the next player picks up.
suggested_fix: Add: 'Don't talk about your own hand during play, such as what you're building or what you're waiting for.' and 'If you want a discard, call it right away, before the next player draws.'

issue: I only read these for rules. I didn't see anything wrong. Mentions of the National Mah Jongg League card and NMJL rules are fine as written.
